Homebrew and uv bring their own Python (uv downloads one when yours is too old), and pipx installed with Homebrew uses Homebrew's. Method Commands Upgrade Homebrew (Apple silicon macOS, Linux) brew tap aashishmahajan/kube-noob https://github.com/aashishmahajan/kube-noob , then brew trust --formula aashishmahajan/kube-noob/kube-noob , then brew install kube-noob brew update && brew upgrade kube-noob uv (downloads a Python if yours is too old) uv tool install kube-noob uv tool upgrade kube-noob pipx pipx install kube-noob pipx upgrade kube-noob pip, in a virtual environment python3.13 -m venv ~/.venvs/kube-noob , then ~/.venvs/kube-noob/bin/pip install kube-noob ~/.venvs/kube-noob/bin/pip install -U kube-noob Container podman run --rm ghcr.io/aashishmahajan/kube-noob:0.7 --version pull the new tag Claude Code plugin /plugin marketplace add aashishmahajan/kube-noob , then /plugin install kube-noob@kube-noob /plugin marketplace update kube-noob The tap is needed because kube-noob is not in Homebrew's main catalogue; after brew tap , brew install kube-noob finds it. Homebrew 6 and later also refuse formulae from third-party taps until you trust them; brew trust --formula trusts only this one formula ( Homebrew: Tap Trust ). Get uv or pipx with brew install uv or brew install pipx . Every method installs two commands: kube-noob and its short form noob (from 0.2.3). The PyPI package named noob is an unrelated graph library that also installs a noob command; if you have it, use kube-noob . Check what you are running: kube-noob --version which -a kube-noob which -a lists every kube-noob on your PATH . If it prints more than one, an older install is shadowing the new one: remove it with the tool that installed it ( pipx uninstall kube-noob , uv tool uninstall kube-noob or brew uninstall kube-noob ). Agent Skill The same tools as the MCP server, as an Agent Skill : a folder with SKILL.md , a runner ( scripts/kn.py , one tool per call, JSON out) and the readable server source the Claude plugin ships. Use it where no MCP server runs: chat on claude.ai (the plugin's local MCP server runs in Claude Code and Cowork only) and the Claude API's code execution. It runs with the offline lock on and needs Python 3.11 or later with pydantic, PyYAML and jsonschema; kn.py check says which are missing. Where Install claude.ai (Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise, with code execution on) Download kube-noob-skill-<version>.zip from the GitHub release (from 0.7.0), then upload it under Customize > Skills and turn it on Claude Code Unzip it into ~/.claude/skills/ (so the file is ~/.claude/skills/kube-noob/SKILL.md ), or install the plugin instead, which also gives the MCP tools From a checkout python scripts/build_skill.py --zip kube-noob-skill.zip or --out ~/.claude/skills/kube-noob Run it yourself to see what Claude sees: python3 -I -B kube-noob/scripts/kn.py check python3 -I -B kube-noob/scripts/kn.py tools python3 -I -B kube-noob/scripts/kn.py insight '{"text": "0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory"}' python3 -I -B kube-noob/scripts/kn.py audit_manifests --text-file manifests=app.yaml Errors and fixes You see Why Fix No available formula with the name "kube-noob" The tap is not added brew tap aashishmahajan/kube-noob https://github.com/aashishmahajan/kube-noob , then brew trust --formula aashishmahajan/kube-noob/kube-noob , then brew install kube-noob Refusing to load formula aashishmahajan/kube-noob/kube-noob from untrusted tap Homebrew 6 requires trust for third-party taps brew trust --formula aashishmahajan/kube-noob/kube-noob , then brew install kube-noob Requires-Python >=3.11.4 and No matching distribution found for kube-noob Your python3 is older than 3.11 Use Homebrew, uv or pipx above, or a virtual environment made with Python 3.11+ error: externally-managed-environment Homebrew's or the system's Python refuses packages installed into it (PEP 668) Use pipx, uv or a virtual environment; Every demo runs offline in under a second and never touches your cluster or your saved progress: kube-noob demo --list . No AI inside: three ways to use it kube-noob is the rulebook, not the chatbot. Its audit rules, playbooks, docs index and graders give the same answer every time, and they run where you put them. With Claude (plugin in Claude Code or Cowork): ask in your own words and paste YAML, events or logs. Claude calls kube-noob's tools and explains the results. Your conversation goes to Claude as usual; kube-noob sends nothing. With OpenShift Lightspeed or another MCP client : the same tools, served in your cluster ( openshift.md ). That client's model does the talking. With no AI at all : the CLI below. Audits, diagnoses, cited search, lessons and evidence bundles need no model and no network, which suits CI gates and air-gapped clusters. kube-noob ask is the one optional command that uses a model: one you configure, and only a local one under the offline lock. Learner or trainer: practise Kubernetes objects offline You write YAML and get graded feedback straight away. The grader uses the same rules as a production review, and it knows the platform: an SCC rejection on OpenShift, a storage class on ROSA HCP. kube-noob demo learn kube-noob learn tracks kube-noob learn lesson k8s-101-objects kube-noob learn exercise k8s-ex-hardened-deployment kube-noob learn submit k8s-ex-hardened-deployment -f my-answer.yaml The learning guide covers running a class. Developer: ship YAML that passes on OpenShift and ROSA HCP kube-noob demo audit kube-noob audit -f k8s/ --platform openshift --version 4.22 kube-noob fix -f k8s/deployment.yaml --platform openshift -o fixed.yaml kube-noob protocol "deploy orders-api" --blueprint examples/blueprint.yaml kube-noob helm-chart --name orders-api --namespace shop --image quay.io/acme/orders:1.4.2 --platform rosa-hcp -o charts To gate pull requests, run kube-noob audit -f k8s/ --fail-on high in CI. It exits 1 on any HIGH or CRITICAL finding. SRE or on-call: diagnose before you change anything Not sure what you have? insight names it first (events, logs, a denial, manifests, a ticket, a build log, a question; several at once), runs every analyser that applies and merges the answer: findings with their source, read-only next steps, and what it did not analyse and why. Input with no evidence gets the read-only commands that collect some. A document is related reading for a long pasted post only when it shares words with the post beyond the name of its subject: every Gatekeeper post says "gatekeeper". kube-noob insight -f whatever-you-copied.txt oc describe pod web-1 -n shop | kube-noob insight --platform openshift kube-noob insight 'why does my pod stay Pending?' kube-noob insight -f trace.pcap --format json Paste events, describe output or logs into diagnose : as quoted text (multi-line is fine; single quotes stop the shell expanding $ ), as a file with -f , or piped in. An Alertmanager webhook payload works as it is. You get the signals it found (alert names, event and container reasons), the likely cause, then read-only steps (get, describe, logs, events). Commands that run inside a container are listed next, and changes come last. Both are marked as needing approval. kube-noob demo diagnose kube-noob diagnose 'Back-off restarting failed container api in pod api-1' kube-noob diagnose -f events.txt kube-noob diagnose -f alert.json kube-noob signals -f alert.json oc get events -n shop --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | kube-noob diagnose kube-noob bundle deployment/orders-api -n shop --cluster-enabled Signals rank the playbooks: a firing etcdHighNumberOfLeaderChanges puts the etcd playbook first even when the words differ, and a payload's openshift_version (or version ) label, when it names an OpenShift 4 release, picks the reported issues for that version. signals (MCP: kubenoob_extract_signals ) lists what was found, the alerts the words imply ("leader changed"), each catalogue entry's upstream source and the playbooks they point at. An ImagePullBackOff whose pull secret sits in another namespace is named for what it is: kubelet's FailedToRetrieveImagePullSecret event (or the question in those words) ranks the pull-secret playbook first, with the secret and namespace filled in, read-only checks that list Secret names (never values), and the cause the words point at shown first with its own fix and steps: a secret in another namespace gets "create or sync it in the pod's namespace and link it" and kubectl get secrets -A --field-selector metadata.name=<secret> ; only a question that says OpenShift and names another project's internal registry gets system:image-puller . The 17 playbooks that answer most real posts work this way (cause-linked triage): each cause carries the words that point at it, the read-only steps that confirm it and its fixes, and text that never says OpenShift gets kubectl steps. Writing YAML and getting precise feedback teaches the habits. kube-noob closes that loop offline: Graded by production rules. Exercises are checked by the 60-rule audit engine and the strict schemas that review real manifests. A passing answer is one a platform team would accept. Platform-aware. The same Deployment is right on Kubernetes and wrong on OpenShift (fixed runAsUser against restricted-v2 ) or on ROSA HCP (storage class, Routes). Learners see why. Cited. Lessons and feedback point to credited sources ( [kn:<doc>#<n>] ), so learners know where each rule comes from. No cluster, no cloud bill, no network. It runs on a laptop, in a classroom or on an air-gapped machine. The curriculum has 5 tracks (Kubernetes, OpenShift, ROSA HCP, Helm, RHACS/StackRox), with 16 lessons, 9 graded exercises and 15 quiz questions. Running a class pipx install kube-noob kube-noob learn tracks --learner alice kube-noob learn lesson k8s-101-objects --learner alice kube-noob learn exercise k8s-ex-hardened-deployment kube-noob learn submit k8s-ex-hardened-deployment -f answer.yaml --learner alice kube-noob learn progress --learner alice Each learner earns credits for passing exercises and quizzes. Progress lives in their data directory. A submission exits 0 when it passes, so instructors can grade a folder of answers in a script. In Claude, the tutor prompt runs the same loop conversationally, one concept at a time. Running kube-noob as a shared server for a whole class (one deployment, several learners connecting over HTTP)? Every caller must pass its own learner ; the server refuses the CLI's single-user "local" default so no learner's progress is ever silently shared with another's. Start with kube-noob demo learn to see a full lesson-and-grade cycle in seconds. What kube-noob remembers kube-noob keeps a small local file, <dataDir>/learning.json . By default that is ~/.local/share/kube-noob/learning.json , or /var/lib/kube-noob in the container with persistence enabled. Kept How it gets there Profile: platform, versions, team conventions you state it ( kube-noob learning profile , or the learning_profile_set tool) Notes: symptom, cause, fix only after you confirm a fix worked ( kube-noob learning note , learning_note_add ) Counters: which playbooks, rules and platforms come up automatic; ids only, never content It never keeps raw logs, manifests, credentials, cluster objects or conversations. Notes that look like any of these are rejected. Search. Notes appear in search results and can be cited as [kn:local-N#0] . Training data. Notes are never exported as training data. Agent context. The agent adds your profile to its context. Upgrade-safe. The file lives outside the installed package, so upgrading the CLI, the plugin or the image keeps it. schemaVersion migrates older files forward and keeps keys written by newer versions. A file from a newer version opens read-only. A corrupt file is moved aside, never overwritten. kube-noob learning show kube-noob learning profile --platform rosa-hcp --openshift 4.22 --convention "namespaces are <team>-<env>" kube-noob learning note --symptom "..." --cause "..." --fix "..." kube-noob learning forget local-3 To turn it off, set learningEnabled: false or KUBE_NOOB_LEARNING_ENABLED=false . To back it up, copy the file. Source: docs/learning.md

All three serve the same MCP tools, and all three start offline and read-only. Mode Who calls it Network exposure When to use Service (Helm chart) MCP clients and OpenShift Lightspeed, over HTTP with a bearer token ClusterIP; optional Route One shared instance for a team or the whole cluster Sidecar Only containers in the same pod, on 127.0.0.1 none Your own bot or agent that needs Kubernetes expertise OpenShift Lightspeed tool Lightspeed's chat in the console calls the Service in-cluster only Developers ask in the console; kube-noob supplies audits, diagnoses and cited answers 1. Service mode oc new-project kube-noob oc create secret generic kube-noob-token --from-literal=token="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" helm install kube-noob deploy/helm/kube-noob -n kube-noob --set auth.existingSecret=kube-noob-token --set config.offline=true --set config.defaultPlatform=rosa-hcp oc rollout status deployment/kube-noob -n kube-noob helm test kube-noob -n kube-noob config.offline=true is the admin lock: no web, no corpus downloads, local models only. The pod runs under restricted-v2 . NetworkPolicies allow only the same namespace and the router by default. Egress allows DNS only. Read-only cluster evidence ( cluster_get , cluster_debug_workload ) is opt-in. Set --set config.clusterEnabled=true --set "rbac.namespaces={shop,payments}" and list the API server CIDRs in networkPolicy.egress.apiServerCIDRs . The ServiceAccount gets read verbs only, never Secrets, and by default only in its own namespace plus rbac.namespaces ; rbac.scope=cluster widens that. Every holder of the token reads through this ServiceAccount, so grant only the namespaces its users may see. Over HTTP, tools that write the learning file are not offered, because callers share one file. Add team notes with oc exec deploy/kube-noob -- kube-noob learning note ... (with persistence.enabled=true and replicaCount=1 ). Persist notes, corpus and progress with --set persistence.enabled=true --set replicaCount=1 (a ReadWriteOnce volume attaches to one node, so the chart uses one replica and the Recreate strategy with it). Your own runbooks: kube-noob corpus add-docs <folder> --source platform-runbooks indexes them wherever the CLI or plugin runs. Loading runbooks into the in-cluster service (an init container that reads a Git repo or a ConfigMap) is on the roadmap. Clients connect to http://kube-noob.kube-noob.svc:8080/mcp with Authorization: Bearer <token> . Callers that do not speak MCP (CI jobs, scripts, a chat bot) use the REST routes beside it, with the same token and the same tools: POST /v1/insight , /v1/diagnose , /v1/audit , /v1/known-issues , /v1/policy/reach , /v1/memory/match (with memory.source ), /v1/must-gather (with mustGather.pvc.claimName ), and GET or POST /v1/reports . GET /v1/openapi.json describes them ( docs/api/openapi.json ); GET /v1 lists the routes this install offers. Bodies are JSON objects with the tool's arguments; a POST must be application/json . curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"text": "0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory."}' http://kube-noob.kube-noob.svc:8080/v1/diagnose 2. Sidecar mode deploy/sidecar/app-with-kube-noob-sidecar.yaml is a complete example. kube-noob listens on 127.0.0.1:8080 inside your pod, so no Service, Route or token is needed. Your container calls http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp . Audit the example with: kube-noob audit -f deploy/sidecar/app-with-kube-noob-sidecar.yaml --platform openshift --fail-on medium 3. OpenShift Lightspeed integration OpenShift Lightspeed can call external MCP servers when the MCPServer feature gate is on. Lightspeed's own model does the talking; kube-noob answers its tool calls with audits, diagnoses and cited docs, and calls no model itself. The field names below come from the OLSConfig API in the lightspeed-operator. Run oc explain olsconfig.spec.mcpServers to confirm the schema of your installed version. Install kube-noob in service mode (section 1), then let the Lightspeed namespace reach it: helm upgrade kube-noob deploy/helm/kube-noob -n kube-noob --reuse-values --set networkPolicy.allowIngressNamespace=openshift-lightspeed Give Lightspeed the bearer token. The operator reads the header value from the key header of a Secret in its own namespace: oc create secret generic kube-noob-mcp-auth -n openshift-lightspeed --from-literal=header="Bearer $(oc get secret kube-noob-token -n kube-noob -o jsonpath='{.data.token}' | base64 -d)" Register the server and turn on the gate: apiVersion: ols.openshift.io/v1alpha1 kind: OLSConfig metadata: name: cluster spec: featureGates: - MCPServer mcpServers: - name: kube-noob url: http://kube-noob.kube-noob.svc:8080/mcp timeout: 30 headers: - name: Authorization valueFrom: type: secret secretRef: name: kube-noob-mcp-auth Merge this into your existing OLSConfig with oc edit olsconfig cluster . Python dependency CVE with a fix pip-audit on requirements.lock yes, patch Fixable HIGH/CRITICAL CVE in the released image Trivy on ghcr.io/aashishmahajan/kube-noob:<latest> yes, patch (rebuild) Upstream release newer than verified knowledge Kubernetes, OpenShift, Helm, StackRox vs scripts/risk_baseline.json yes, after re-verifying facts New mcp or anthropic SDK PyPI vs lock pins review; release only if behaviour changes Unfixed CVE (no fix yet) pip-audit / Trivy review, document, no release Procedure Open the latest risk-review issue (or run gh workflow run risk-review.yml ). For each reason, make the fix on main : - dependency: uv pip compile pyproject.toml --generate-hashes --python-version 3.12 --universal --upgrade-package <pkg> -o requirements.lock - image: no code change needed; the release rebuilds on the current UBI digest - drift: re-verify the affected facts against the source, update knowledge, catalog and tests, then bump scripts/risk_baseline.json Verify locally: scripts/check.sh (plugin copy, lint, types, tests, self-test). Bump and changelog: python scripts/bump_version.py <next> "<one-line reason>" . Commit, push, and wait for CI to pass on main . Tag and push: git tag v<next> && git push origin v<next> . The release workflow publishes to PyPI (trusted publishing), pushes the signed multi-arch image and the signed OCI Helm chart to GHCR, publishes to the MCP Registry and creates the GitHub release with the chart .tgz and demo GIFs. After PyPI shows the version: python scripts/brew_formula.py <next> --write , commit and push; the brew workflow installs it on macOS and Linux. Close the weekly issue with the release link. Tags must be pushed by a person or the scheduled agent: tags pushed with the workflow GITHUB_TOKEN do not trigger other workflows. The Claude plugin directory reads the plugin ( .claude-plugin/marketplace.json and plugin/kube-noob/ ) from main , and its review shows the commit it last checked. Work done on another branch reaches it only after that branch is merged to main and someone presses "Check for new commits" (or sets up push updates) in the plugin portal. A version that is bumped on main but never tagged never reaches PyPI, the image or the MCP Registry: 0.5.0 (073fe80) was bumped on main and not tagged, so PyPI stopped at 0.4.0. Rollback PyPI versions are immutable. Yank the bad version ( pypi.org/manage/project/kube-noob/releases/ ), fix forward, and release the next patch. GHCR: delete or retag the bad image version; users pinned by digest are unaffected. MCP Registry and the Claude plugin follow the next published version. Escalation Vulnerability reports arrive through GitHub private vulnerability reporting (see SECURITY.md ); acknowledge within 3 business days. A failing release workflow blocks the release: fix and re-tag with the next patch version (never reuse a version). Source: docs/operations.md

No AI inside: Claude does the thinking; kube-noob supplies the audit rules, read-only-first troubleshooting steps, cited docs and graded exercises, and runs on your computer. Design and review requests follow a 7-step protocol: Clarify, Validate, Research, Audit, Calibrate, Generate, Red Team. Install In Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add aashishmahajan/kube-noob /plugin install kube-noob@kube-noob In claude.ai or the Claude desktop app: Customize > Plugins > Add > Add marketplace , enter aashishmahajan/kube-noob , then add kube-noob from the list. It is saved to your account and also reaches Claude Code. The tools run on your computer, so they work in Claude Code and in Cowork sessions on your computer; in a chat conversation only the skills load. The server needs uv ( brew install uv or pipx install uv ). How to use it Ask Claude in your own words; the skills route the work to kube-noob's tools. "Review this Deployment for OpenShift 4.22" and paste the YAML: findings with line numbers, fixes and the RHACS policy each one would trip. "My pod is in CrashLoopBackOff" and paste oc describe pod or the events: the likely cause, then read-only checks first; anything that changes the cluster comes last and needs your approval. "Write manifests for orders-api on ROSA HCP with shared storage": audited YAML through the 7-step protocol. "Is this a known bug?" with an OpenShift error: the matching issue from the release notes, its link, the version that fixes it and the workaround. "Why was this denied?" with a Kyverno, Gatekeeper, Pod Security, SCC, quota or RBAC error, or "can frontend reach orders-api on 8080?": the policy and rule that decided it, the field that failed and the fix. "Teach me Services" or "give me an exercise": lessons and graded exercises. Commands in an answer are for you to run: the skills tell Claude to hand them to you rather than run them, and kube-noob itself never changes your cluster. How it runs Claude Code starts the server with uv run --frozen --isolated against the readable Python source in server/ , installing the dependencies at the exact versions and SHA-256 hashes in the uv.lock beside this file into a throwaway environment in uv's cache. -I keeps your working directory and PYTHONPATH off sys.path , and -B writes no .pyc into the plugin. If no Python 3.11 or later is present, uv downloads its managed CPython once. Nothing else is downloaded and no LLM SDK is installed. A pinned package launcher — uvx kube-noob==<version> mcp — is what the plugin directory clears automatically, where uv run --frozen is held for a human reviewer. It becomes the default from 0.7.1, not before: the published 0.7.0 has no switch to withhold analyze_must_gather , the one tool that opens a path on your machine rather than reading text it was handed, so installing the published package would hand the plugin a capability the vendored copy has never had. 0.7.1 adds mustGather.enabled , this file already sets KUBE_NOOB_MUST_GATHER_ENABLED=false , and the two launchers then offer exactly the same tools. What the vendored copy is The server source in server/ is the modules of the kube-noob repository 's src/kube_noob that the stdio MCP server imports, copied unchanged. The CLI, the optional model agent, the HTTP service and REST routes, the web client, Helm rendering and the cluster backends are not included, so nothing in that copy reads a credential, opens a connection or starts another program. Beside it is a uv.lock pinning every dependency to an exact version and SHA-256 hash. From 0.7.1 the default becomes the pinned package launcher. To keep running this vendored copy instead — on an air-gapped machine, or when you want every dependency fixed by hash rather than resolved at install time — keep the mcpServers entry as: {"command": "uv", "args": ["run", "--frozen", "--exact", "--isolated", "--quiet", "--project", "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}", "python", "-I", "-B", "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/server/kube_noob_plugin.py"]} That form reads only the source in this directory and the hashes in uv.lock , and resolves nothing at install time. It stays the stronger of the two. Vendoring mcp , pydantic , starlette and uvicorn as well — which would let the plugin run a plain file with no resolver at all — does not fit the directory's file-count and file-size limits. What it accesses Network: none of its own. The plugin has no web client and no cluster access, and the server never calls a model; uv's one-time install of the pinned dependencies is the only download. Files: stores learning progress and learning.json (your platform, versions, conventions and the fixes you confirmed; never logs, manifests or secrets) in ~/.local/share/kube-noob , which survives plugin upgrades. To read your cluster (read-only, never Secrets) or allowlisted documentation sites, use the kube-noob CLI ( pipx install kube-noob ) or the in-cluster service; the plugin stays offline. Asks you for nothing and reads nothing out of your environmen

The server, the CLI and the plugin run deterministic code: rules, schemas, playbooks, a BM25 index and graders. A model appears only on the client side (Claude, Lightspeed, any MCP client) or in the optional kube-noob ask agent, which calls the same toolkit. Request flow (run_protocol) Clarify - platform/version inference (blueprint > explicit > request text > manifest API groups), blocking questions vs stated assumptions. Validate - strict JSON schema (Kubernetes 1.35 + CRDs), apiVersion/kind catalog, removed APIs per target version, selector/port wiring. Research - BM25 over local knowledge; results carry chunk ids, source URLs and licenses. Audit - security, RBAC, network exposure, storage access modes vs provisioner capabilities. Calibrate - probes, resources, replicas, PDBs, topology spread, HPA prerequisites. Generate - deterministic generator (blueprints) or mechanical fixer (existing YAML) with a change log. Red Team - nine adversarial scenarios evaluated on the final output; remaining HIGH/CRITICAL findings mark the result blocked . Trust boundaries MCP clients and model output are untrusted input: every tool validates with Pydantic, YAML is size/alias bounded. Text that came from outside is untrusted on the way out too: kube_noob.sanitize cleans every MCP result (invisible characters, role and tool-call markers, instruction phrases, exfiltrating Markdown) and flags it untrusted . Pasted payloads are data too: an Alertmanager payload is read as JSON only (2 MB, 500 alerts, 64 labels, 2,000 characters per value, control characters dropped), and only an OpenShift release label sets the version. The Agent Skill ( skill/kube-noob/scripts/kn.py ) is a fourth surface over the same toolkit: it calls kube_noob.tool_runner.call (the code path mcp_app.run_tool uses), loads only the bundled copy of the server source next to it, and forces offline: true , web and cluster off and no model, whatever the config file or KUBE_NOOB_* variables say. Its trust boundary is the model that runs it: arguments are validated by the tool's model, input is capped at 5 MiB, and results are cleaned and flagged like MCP results. The HTTP transport authenticates with a bearer token (constant time) unless bound to loopback (sidecar). REST routes ( kube_noob.server.rest , /v1/... ) sit beside MCP on the same app and run the same toolkit call ( mcp_app.run_tool : validation, sanitising, knowledgeAsOf , the content-free audit line, now with via=rest ). Trust boundary: the caller holding the token. They pass the bearer check and body limit first, then the MCP transport's Host and Origin checks; a POST must be application/json , so a cross-site form cannot reach a tool. Only the tools the shared server offers have routes. docs/api/openapi.json is generated from the tools' models ( scripts/gen_openapi.py ) and a test keeps it equal to the code. Outbound HTTP only through kube_noob.net : web purpose requires webEnabled and allowlisted HTTPS hosts on every hop, GET only; web_fetch refuses non-text content types before reading the body. LLM and in-cluster API clients are separate, explicit purposes. The admin lock ( offline: true ) is applied at config load and only tightens: it disables web, refuses corpus downloads and allows only loopback or *.svc model endpoints. kube-noob doctor reports the result. Cluster access is read-only, allowlisted per resource, never Secrets, and redacts values before they reach a model. Diagnoses list read-only steps first; commands that execute or change state are labelled as needing approval. A structured playbook ties each root cause to the patterns that point at it, its own read-only steps and fixes ( debug.playbooks.Cause , debug.diagnose.likely_cause ); with no pattern matching, the first cause is shown. Names in steps come only from command-shaped input ( pod/<name> , kubectl get svc <name> , Selector: lines) and are pasted into a command only when made of characters a shell leaves alone there, so a copied step only ever reads. Anything beyond reading is a capability tier ( kube_noob.tiers : probe, dry-run, external writes, gate forwarding), off by default. Code that changes something is a Writer that cannot be built while its tier is off, and each action needs a person's Approval for that action, unexpired and used once. The read-only backends have no write method; tier RBAC renders only when the tier is on. A memory repository ( kube_noob.memory ) is the team's own Git content: kube-noob reads it locally, writes only on memory init , add , outcome and migrate-learning (new files created exclusively, rewrites atomic), never runs git, and never bundles, publishes or exports it. Entries are untrusted input until memory validate passes: bounded YAML, content rules, and the verifier on every fix (validate, audit and red team on patches; privileged SCC, cluster-admin, hostPath and wildcard RBAC grants fail without a recorded risk acceptance). Do not open a public issue. Expect an acknowledgement within 3 business days and a fix or mitigation plan within 30 days for confirmed issues. Supported versions The latest minor release receives security fixes. Default posture kube-noob makes no outbound connections and touches no cluster unless you enable it. This is tested in CI and was verified end to end inside a network namespace with no route (docs/release-readiness.md). With web access enabled it only performs HTTPS GETs to allowlisted documentation domains, refuses non-text content types (archives, binaries, scripts), streams at most web.maxBytes , never writes the content to disk and never executes it. The admin lock ( offline: true / KUBE_NOOB_OFFLINE=1 ) overrides webEnabled , blocks corpus downloads and allows only loopback or in-cluster model endpoints; no later configuration source can lift it. kube-noob doctor reports the effective posture. The local learning file stores only user-confirmed summaries and ids, never logs, manifests or credentials. The MCP server's only subprocesses are read-only oc / kubectl calls (argv, no shell) when cluster access is enabled; the maintainer CLI commands corpus build --online and helm-audit run git and helm template locally. The Agent Skill ( skill/kube-noob ) cannot be configured out of this posture: its runner forces the offline lock, web and cluster off and no model on every call, ignoring the config file and KUBE_NOOB_* variables, imports the bundled server source only (it refuses another installed kube-noob), and its tools start no other program and open no connection (a test runs them with both refused). Security design Area Control Network webEnabled: false by default; all outbound HTTP goes through one guarded client; web requests (and every redirect) must be HTTPS to an allowlisted domain. Cluster access Opt-in ( cluster.enabled ), read-only verbs on an allowlist of resources, Secrets never readable, ConfigMap values / sensitive env values / token-like log content redacted, strict argument validation, no shell. HTTP server Refuses to bind non-loopback without a bearer token (constant-time compare, and two Authorization headers are refused rather than resolved last-wins) unless explicitly overridden; DNS-rebinding protection with a Host allowlist; health endpoints are the only unauthenticated paths. The body limit is 1.5 MiB, below the 1,000,000-character argument cap so no valid request is refused, and a body on the public health paths is refused with 405 before it is buffered, so an unauthenticated caller cannot make the server hold memory. The REST routes ( /v1/... ) are behind the same token and body limit, pass the same Host and Origin checks, accept only application/json posts, and exist only for the tools the shared server offers (none that writes). Input parsing YAML SafeLoader only, 5 MB / 1000-document caps, alias-expansion budget against billion-laughs. Suggested commands Steps a diagnosis prints are read-only and copy-paste safe: a name taken from the input (pod, Service, label selector, namespace) is pasted into a command only when it is made of letters, digits and @._:/=+#%,- and does not start with # , otherwise its placeholder stays; a Service selector is used only when every key and value is a valid label; no step prints a Secret's values. Every validator ends with \Z , not $ (Python's $ also matches before a final newline, so a must-gather namespace "shop\n" once split a printed step into two shell lines); a test fails on any new validator anchored with $ . Must-gathers Opened as a stream or a walk with no links followed; nothing extracted or run; Secrets-named files never read; YAML pre-scanned for aliases, documents and depth before libyaml loads it. The analyze_must_gather MCP tool is offered by the HTTP server only with mustGather.allowedDir and reads only paths that resolve inside it (links resolved first); it is not in the Claude plugin. Prompt injection Every MCP tool result and the knowledge resource is cleaned before it leaves the server. Removed: invisible Unicode (tags, bidi overrides, zero-width other than an emoji's joiner, soft hyphens and other word splitters), chat-template and role markers, tool-call markup, instructions aimed at a model (matched on a normalised copy: full-width and mathematical letters folded, Cyrillic and Greek look-alikes mapped, entities and colour codes decoded, hyphenated line breaks joined; English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Russian, Chinese, Japanese, Korean; inside base64), every remote image address and a link's query when it can carry data. Flagged but kept: phrases that are operations as often as attacks ("send the credentials to vault.example.com"). The result carries untrusted: true and the signals. Evals: 66 of 66 and 25 of 25 with no finding on 148 benign lines; the red team's 50 new attacks 48 caught and its 55

FedRAMP authorizes cloud service offerings, so kube-noob counts as a component of the offering it runs in (for example an OpenShift or ROSA cluster in a FedRAMP High environment), and the controls below are met by how that offering deploys and operates it. This page says what kube-noob gives as evidence, how to deploy it inside a High boundary, and what is not covered yet. Researched 2026-10-27. FedRAMP is changing: the Consolidated Rules for 2026 apply to every authorization from 1 January 2027, and the Vulnerability Detection and Response rules from 7 December 2026 for obtaining and for maintaining a certification, with a grace period to 7 March 2027. 20x Class D (the high-impact class) is not in pilot yet: RFC-0033 proposes the Phase 4 pilot for FY27 Q1 and Q2, with the application window 1-4 December 2026 and a cap of ten participants, and applicants need a CR26-compliant Class C certification first (checked 2026-10-31). Both Rev5 baselines and the 20x Key Security Indicators are written against NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 controls, which is what kube-noob maps to. keep the chart's NetworkPolicy (DNS-only egress) and add the EgressFirewall on OVN-Kubernetes SC-13 Install OpenShift in FIPS mode and use the UBI-based image: kube-noob uses only SHA-256 and the system OpenSSL, so its crypto runs in the validated module. kube-noob doctor must show FIPS mode on AC-3, AC-6 Live cluster access stays off unless needed; when on it is read-only, namespace-scoped, never reads Secrets and redacts values IA-2, IA-5, AC-2 Put the HTTP service behind the OpenShift OAuth proxy backed by your PIV/CAC identity provider instead of relying only on the shared bearer token AU-2, AU-3, AU-12 Ship the container's stdout to cluster logging and your SIEM: each tool call logs the tool, argument sizes, outcome and duration, never content SI-7, SR-11 Deploy by digest from your mirror and verify the cosign signature and provenance before admission (RHACS or a Sigstore admission policy) RA-5, SI-2 Scan the image in your registry (RHACS, Quay, Clair) and fix within the Vulnerability Detection and Response timeframes; Measured on the real server: 70 idle sockets, still 503 after 16 seconds, recovering only when they close. kube-noob cannot close that in process, so the parts it does own are now consistent with it. Buffered-body memory is the concurrency limit times the body limit, and that product used to be 64 x 8 MiB = 512 MiB against a 512Mi container -- exactly the ceiling the kernel kills at; with the 1.5 MiB limit it is 96 MiB, and a test keeps the two numbers from drifting apart again. The liveness probe is now four times more forgiving than readiness (120s against 30s), so sustained overload takes the pod out of the endpoints instead of restarting a pod whose restart frees no connection and drops the work in flight. And SECURITY.md states the limitation: expose the port through a proxy, ingress or mesh that enforces a header-read and idle timeout. The default sidecar binds 127.0.0.1, where only containers in the same pod can reach it. A shared server offered three tools that wrote per-caller state it had no identity to key on. The filter meant to keep write tools off the HTTP server was a denylist of three names, and three more had been added since: learn_lesson , learn_submit and learn_quiz each wrote progress/<learner>.json . The server has one static bearer token, so the learner id comes from the caller and binds to nothing -- the red team showed one caller's wrong answer taking the credit for another's right one, and anybody reading anybody's tally. The filter is now the read_only flag each tool already carries, so a write tool added later is excluded by construction. The three tools stay on the shared server and grade, mark and teach identically, but record nothing and say so in the result; learn_progress returns no tally there rather than one anyone could have written. That makes the old SAFE2 guard -- which refused the "local" learner id on a shared server -- pointless, so it is gone: it only caught the caller who forgot to pass an id, never the one who passed somebody else's. A local progress file is read and written under a lock. Fifteen concurrent answers used to store between two and eight of them, because load and save took none; one person with two clients open is enough for that, and a lost credit is a silent wrong answer. An unauthenticated caller could kill the HTTP server through its health endpoints. /healthz and /readyz skip the bearer token so the kubelet can probe them, and skipped it for every method -- while the body limit sat inside the auth middleware and buffered up to 8 MiB per connection before the router answered 405. Fifty such connections took the process from 96 MiB to 522 MiB, and in a 512Mi cgroup matching the chart's own limit the kernel killed it. A probe sends no body, so a body on those paths is now refused before it is read. The comment claiming "a caller without the token cannot make the server buffer requests" was false, and is now true. The request body limit was six times larger than any valid request. Every tool argument is capped at 1,000,000 characters, so an 8 MiB body could never succeed -- but it was buffered, copied by request.body() , copied again by the decode, and then bracket-scanned in pure Python, which stalled the event loop for 0.41s per body and up to 7.9s under load, against the chart's 3s probe timeout. The limit is 1.5 MiB, which still leaves room for JSON-RPC framing around a maximum-length argument. The JSON nesting guard checked a different string from the one the parser read. json.loads accepts bytes and sniffs UTF-16 and UTF-32, while the guard counted brackets on a UTF-8 decoding of those bytes -- and a backslash followed by a NUL desynchronises in-string tracking, so {"s": "a\"b", "d": [[[...]]]} in UTF-16 passed a guard that refused the same text in UTF-8. The guard exists because deep nesting overflows the C stack on CPython 3.14 as a fatal error rather than a RecursionError , so a bypass of it is the whole defect. The body is now decoded once, by the same rule the parser uses, and only that string is counted and parsed. A legitimate UTF-16 body is still understood rather than refused. Two Authorization headers are refused instead of resolved. dict(scope["headers"]) keeps the last value while a proxy in front reads the first, so "wrong, right" authenticated and "right, wrong" did not. Neither resolution is the right one for a request that is never legitimate. The audit line is documented as content-free -- "which tool, argument names and sizes" -- and on the REST path the names come from the caller's body before it is validated. One request with an 8 MiB key name wrote an 18 MiB log line and spent 9s of CPU. Names are truncated and the count capped, with the number dropped recorded. The shared server rebuilt the whol

The Jira pull is jittered and rate-limited, keeps no identities, and scrubs emails and account ids. For non-public projects set JIRA_EMAIL and JIRA_API_TOKEN (sent over HTTPS only). Copyleft, non-commercial, unlicensed and Jira content is redistributable: false : usable for local retrieval and private evaluation, excluded from exports unless you pass --include-restricted . Air-gapped clusters: kube-noob corpus import corpus.tgz (names and checksums are verified before import). The corpus-refresh workflow rebuilds everything weekly in GitHub Actions. Export datasets and grade kube-noob train export --out dataset/ kube-noob train grade --task bench-qa-rwx-gp3 -f answer.md kube-noob train bench --out report.json train export writes sft.jsonl (chat format) and grpo_prompts.jsonl . The held-out benchmark ( src/kube_noob/data/evals/tasks.yaml ) is never exported. Exports contain no LLM-generated labels. The reward (enforcer and credit system) reward = 0.70 * task + 0.20 * credit * task + 0.10 * format - penalties task : manifest answers are graded by the audit engine plus field assertions that encode the task's intent; a failed assertion or forbidden rule caps the task score at 0.4. QA answers need affirmative claims (negated mentions do not count), any known-wrong claim scores 0, and answers under minWords are scaled down. credit : share of [kn:...] citations that exist and support the answer (task-declared docs, top hits for the prompt, or lexical support of the citing sentence). Credit only counts in proportion to correctness. penalties : fabricated citations, refusals, runaway length. Use it with TRL: GRPOTrainer(reward_funcs=[kube_noob.evals.reward.trl_reward], ...) and a task_id dataset column. The eval-only LLM judge ( judge.provider ) is for spot checks; its output is never exported as a label. Serve a fine-tuned model Point the agent at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (vLLM, Ollama, llama.cpp, OpenShift AI model serving): llm: provider: openai-compatible baseUrl: http://kube-noob-model.ai.svc:8000/v1 model: kube-noob-8b apiKeyEnv: VLLM_API_KEY apiKeyEnv is the only variable the model client reads for openai-compatible , and there is no fallback: without it the request carries no Authorization header. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is the default for llm.provider: anthropic alone, so pointing baseUrl at a gateway cannot quietly hand that key to a third party. Then compare it with a frontier baseline: install the SDK with pipx install 'kube-noob[ask]' , set llm.provider: anthropic and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , and run kube-noob train bench --out report.json . No model is configured by default. Source: docs/training.md

First, a terminology correction There is no longer anything called "the OpenShift marketplace" that a maintainer can submit to. This is the procedure to run on a change worth more than a typo, and the rubric for deciding what to do with what it finds. Why this exists: what 0.7.0 shipped data/ceph_health.yaml held 195 scalars of the form src: [healthmon:885] . A colon with no space after it inside a flow sequence is ambiguous YAML. PyYAML's own scanner reads it as the string "healthmon:885" ; the stricter libyaml in the browser runtime refuses the document outright. signals/ceph.py prefers CSafeLoader when libyaml is present, and signals.catalogue() is on the path of both diagnose and known_issues , so those two tools raised a ScannerError for every visitor to kube-noob.com's playground and for any install whose libyaml is the strict one. scripts/check.sh was green throughout. It had to be: it parses that file with the parser installed on the machine running it, which is the permissive one. Every test asked "does this work here?" and none asked "does this work where we ship it?" The lesson is not that the tests were too few. It is that kube-noob ships to four runtimes and tests in one. A PyPI wheel on the user's Python, a plugin under uv run with locked dependencies, a UBI9 container, and a wheel compiled to WebAssembly in a browser. Anything that reads "whatever is installed" is a place those four can disagree. The three passes Run them in parallel, on cheap models; they are independent. Each brief below is a shape, not a script: fill in the change under review. What makes them produce signal rather than prose is the last rule in each — a finding is not a finding until it names an input and an environment. 1. Environment divergence. Give the model the four runtimes explicitly and the incident above as the worked example, then ask it to find every other place behaviour depends on what happens to be installed: an optional C accelerator, sys.platform , sys.version_info , a try: import fallback, locale, timezone, default encoding, filesystem case sensitivity, line endings, and in the WebAssembly target the absence of threads, subprocesses and sockets. Demand, for each: file and line, what differs, and a concrete input that behaves differently in which runtime. 2. Adversarial review of the diff. Give the model the diff and what it was meant to achieve, and tell it its job is to find what is wrong with it. The axes that paid off: construct an input the new test misses (a false negative); construct a legitimate input it wrongly rejects (a false positive, which blocks future honest changes); verify independently that a data change did not alter meaning; and for anything touching CI, hunt shell quoting, a trigger that cannot fire, a schedule that does not mean what its comment says, and an injection path from attacker-influenced input. Ask what companion fix the author skipped — that question has a good hit rate. 3. Mechanical data sweep. A bounded, exhaustive task suits the cheapest model. Write the script, walk every bundled file, report every value whose type is not what the author plainly meant, then triage. YAML 1.1 coercion is the standing trap here: yes / no / on / off becoming booleans, 1:30 becoming 90, a leading zero becoming octal, and — the one that would really hurt a Kubernetes tool — 4.20 becoming the float 4.2 , a different release. Keep each pass read-only. Let it report; do the fixing yourself, where the judgement is. What it actually found, the day it was written Pass 2, reviewing the fix for the incident above, found three real defects in that fix: a release: published trigger that can never fire, because GitHub starts no workflow for a release created with GITHUB_TOKEN ; a drift alarm whose grace period was shorter than the fallback it was watching, so it would have gone red on about half of all releases by design; and three YAML shapes the new regression test did not catch ( [rule:] , [rule:1, x] ), because PyYAML turns those into a single-pair mapping and the test was only looking at scalars. It also found that the deploy request, as first written, would have fired before the release's videos were attached — reproducing the stale Videos page that prompted the work. All four are fixed. Pass 3 came back almost clean: three non-string values, all benign, no version floats, no tabs, no duplicate keys. A negative result from an exhaustive sweep is worth having and worth recording, so nobody pays for it twice. Ranking what comes out In order. The first question decides most cases. Does it give a wrong answer, silently? An audit or debugging tool that confidently names the wrong cause is worse than one that crashes, because the crash gets reported and the wrong answer gets acted on. Fix first, always, whatever it costs. Does it break a shipped runtime? Weighted by how many users are in that runtime and whether they can tell it is kube-noob's fault. The incident above scored high on both: two of the most-used tools, in the runtime a new visitor meets first. Is

Container keeps crashing (CrashLoopBackOff) DBG-CRASHLOOP · kubernetes, openshift, rosa-classic, rosa-hcp · rules KN-C003 , KN-C005 Likely causes The process exits right after start (bad config, missing env/secret, failed migration, wrong command). Liveness probe kills a slow-starting app (look for 'Liveness probe failed' before each restart). OOMKilled at startup (see lastState.terminated.reason). On OpenShift: the image expects root or a fixed UID and cannot write its directories under the random restricted-v2 UID. CrashLoopBackOff is the waiting state between restarts, not a cause: the kubelet restarts the container with an exponential back-off (10s, 20s, 40s...) capped at 300 seconds, and resets it once the container has run for 10 minutes without a problem. An init container fails (Init:CrashLoopBackOff): the app containers never start, and `logs --previous` without -c shows nothing useful. b: Product journey From a broken pod to a cited, read-only fix kube-noob is the rulebook, not the chatbot. Below is what it does, step by step, with the real output of kube-noob demo from this build: offline, in under a second, never touching a cluster. The 7-step protocol Every design request runs these steps, in this order. Clarify platform/version inference (blueprint > explicit > request text > manifest API groups), blocking questions vs stated assumptions. Validate strict JSON schema (Kubernetes 1.35 + CRDs), apiVersion/kind catalog, removed APIs per target version, selector/port wiring. Research BM25 over local knowledge; results carry chunk ids, source URLs and licenses. Audit security, RBAC, network exposure, storage access modes vs provisioner capabilities. Calibrate probes, resources, replicas, PDBs, topology spread, HPA prerequisites. Generate deterministic generator (blueprints) or mechanical fixer (existing YAML) with a change log. Red Team nine adversarial scenarios evaluated on the final output; remaining HIGH/CRITICAL findings mark the result blocked . What it does, in real output Audit and auto-fix a Deployment for OpenShift For: developers, platform engineers Paste a Deployment and get findings with the line, the fix, the RHACS policy and the NIST controls; fix applies the safe mechanical changes and audits the result again. kube-noob demo audit == kube-noob demo: Audit and auto-fix a Deployment for OpenShift == # Audit a Deployment that works on a laptop but not on OpenShift $ kube-noob audit -f examples/insecure-deployment.yaml --platform openshift --version 4.22 score 37.0/100 | high=3 medium=7 low=5 [HIGH ] KN-S013 line 23: Container 'api' sets DB_PASSWORD as a literal value. fix: Move the value to a Secret and reference it with valueFrom.secretKeyRef (or an external secret store). [HIGH ] KN-S004 line 25: Container 'api' sets runAsUser: 1000; restricted-v2 will reject IDs outside the namespace range. fix: Remove runAsUser/fsGroup and let OpenShift assign IDs from the namespace range; keep runAsNonRoot: true. If a fixed UID is truly required, bind the ServiceAccount to the nonroot-v2 SCC. (runAsGroup is not governed by SCCs and is left alone.) [HIGH ] KN-S002 line 26: Container 'api' explicitly allows privilege escalation. fix: Set securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation: false on every container. # Apply the safe mechanical fixes and re-audit $ kube-noob fix -f examples/insecure-deployment.yaml --platform openshift -o fixed.yaml 5 changes applied; score 37.0 -> 59.0 + spec.template.spec.securityContext.seccompProfile: Pod Security restricted requires RuntimeDefault seccomp. + spec.template.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot: Refuse to start as root. + spec.template.spec.containers[0].securityContext.runAsUser: restricted-v2 assigns IDs from the namespace range. + spec.template.spec.containers[0].securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation: restricted-v2 rejects allowPrivilegeEscalation: true, so the pod could not start anyway. Left for a human (needs app knowledge): - Deployment/shop/orders-api: runAsNonRoot: true was added.
